title: Reverse linked list
prompt: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
explanation: Walk the list once with prev and cur, flipping each next pointer to point backwards.
steps: prev = null, cur = head.
Save next = cur.next, set cur.next = prev, then move both: prev = cur, cur = next.
When cur is null, prev is the new head.
gotcha: Save cur.next before you overwrite it, or you lose the rest of the list.
hint: Walk the list once, flipping each arrow. What do you have to save before flipping one?

title: LRU cache
prompt: Build a fixed-size cache with O(1) get and put that evicts the least recently used key when full.
explanation: You need O(1) lookup and O(1) "which key is oldest?". Classic answer: a hash map pointing into a doubly linked list ordered by use. In JS, a Map already remembers insertion order.
steps: get: if the key exists, delete it and set it again so it moves to the newest end.
put: delete the key if present, then set it.
If size > capacity, delete the oldest key: map.keys().next().value.
gotcha: A get counts as a use too. Forgetting to refresh the key on get is the usual bug.
hint: You need instant lookup plus instant "oldest key". Which structure keeps keys in the order they were added?

title: Word ladder
prompt: Change one letter at a time to get from a start word to an end word, using only words from a list. How many words are in the shortest chain?
explanation: Each word is a node, and words one letter apart are connected. "Shortest" in an unweighted graph means BFS.
steps: Put the word list in a set. Start a queue with [beginWord, 1].
For each word, try every position × every letter a–z. Any result in the set is a neighbor: queue it with length + 1 and remove it from the set.
Return the length when you reach endWord, or 0 if the queue empties.
gotcha: Remove words from the set as you queue them, or BFS revisits them forever. The answer counts words, not steps.
hint: Think of each word as a node. What finds the shortest path when every edge costs the same?

title: Valid palindrome II
prompt: Can the string become a palindrome by deleting at most one character?
explanation: Compare from both ends. At the first mismatch you get one delete: skip the left char or the right char, and check that what's left is a palindrome.
steps: l = 0, r = n - 1. Move inward while s[l] === s[r].
On a mismatch, return isPal(l + 1, r) || isPal(l, r - 1).
If the pointers meet with no mismatch, return true.
gotcha: Try both skips. Picking only one side fails on inputs like "cbbcc".
hint: When the two ends don't match, you get exactly one delete. What are your two options?

title: Sliding window maximum
prompt: For every window of size k sliding across an array, report the window's maximum.
explanation: Keep a deque of indices whose values only decrease. The front is always the window's max. A new value removes everything smaller from the back, because those can never be a max again.
steps: Drop the front index once it falls out of the window.
Pop from the back while those values are ≤ the new value, then push the new index.
Once i ≥ k - 1, record nums[deque[0]].
gotcha: Store indices, not values. You need them to tell when the front has left the window.
hint: A new, bigger number makes the smaller ones before it useless. What do you keep, and in what order?

title: Merge k sorted lists
prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
explanation: The next node in the output is always the smallest current head. A min-heap of the k heads finds it in O(log k).
steps: Push every non-null head into a min-heap keyed by value.
Pop the smallest, attach it to the output, and push its next if there is one.
Repeat until the heap is empty.
gotcha: No heap in JS? Merge the lists in pairs (like merge sort). That's also O(N log k).
hint: At each step you need the smallest of k front nodes. What gives you the minimum quickly?

title: K closest points to origin
prompt: Return the k points nearest to (0, 0).
explanation: This is top-k by distance. Keep a max-heap of size k so the farthest of your current k is on top, ready to be replaced.
steps: Distance = x² + y² (no square root needed).
Push each point. When the heap passes k, pop the farthest.
The heap holds the answer. Quickselect averages O(n).
gotcha: Compare squared distances. Math.sqrt is slower and adds floating-point noise.
hint: Keep only the k best so far. Which of them do you need to compare against each new point?

title: Random pick with weight
prompt: Pick a random index where index i is chosen with probability proportional to w[i].
explanation: Lay the weights end to end as ranges on a number line (prefix sums), throw a random dart, and binary search for the range it lands in.
steps: Build prefix sums: [1, 3, 2] → [1, 4, 6].
Pick r = Math.random() * total.
Binary search for the first prefix sum > r. Its index is the answer.

complexity.time: O(n) setup, O(log n) per pick

gotcha: Use strictly greater than. With ≥, you'll be off by one at range boundaries.
hint: Turn the weights into ranges on a line. How do you find which range a random number falls in?

title: Minimum remove to make valid parentheses
prompt: A string has letters and parentheses. Remove as few parentheses as possible so they're balanced.
explanation: Match brackets with a stack of indices. Any ) with nothing to match, and any ( still on the stack at the end, must go.
steps: On (, push its index. On ), pop if possible. Otherwise mark this index for removal.
After the scan, mark every index left on the stack.
Rebuild the string, skipping the marked indices.
hint: Which brackets end up without a partner? Track the unmatched openers somewhere.

title: Lowest common ancestor of a binary tree
prompt: Find the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree (a node can be its own ancestor).
explanation: Recurse into both sides. If p is found on one side and q on the other, the current node is where they split, so it's the LCA.
steps: If the node is null, p or q, return it.
Recurse left and right.
If both sides return something, this node is the LCA. Otherwise pass up whichever side isn't null.
gotcha: In a BST (LC 235) you can just compare values. In a plain binary tree you need the full DFS.
hint: At which node do p and q end up in different subtrees?

title: Longest palindromic substring
prompt: Find the longest substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation: Every palindrome has a center. Try each one and expand two pointers outward while the characters match. A DP table also works, but uses O(n²) memory.
steps: For each i, expand from (i, i) for odd lengths and (i, i + 1) for even lengths.
Expand while s[l] === s[r].
Keep the longest span you find.
gotcha: Don't forget the even-length centers between characters, like "abba".
hint: Every palindrome is symmetric around a middle. How many possible middles are there?

title: Word break
prompt: Can the string be split into a sequence of words from a dictionary?
explanation: dp[i] = "the first i characters can be split". It's true if some earlier split point j is true and s.slice(j, i) is a word.
steps: dp[0] = true. Put the dictionary in a Set.
For each i, check every j < i: dp[j] && words.has(s.slice(j, i)).
Return dp[n].
gotcha: Plain recursion without memoization is exponential on inputs like "aaaa…b".
hint: If you knew which prefixes can be split, how would you decide about a longer one?

title: Merge two sorted lists
prompt: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
explanation: One pointer per list. Repeatedly attach the smaller head to the output and advance that pointer.
steps: Create a dummy node and a tail pointing at it.
While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller one and advance that list.
Attach whatever remains, then return dummy.next.
gotcha: The dummy node saves you special-casing the first node.
hint: Look only at the front of each list. Which node goes next?

title: Group anagrams
prompt: Group a list of words so that anagrams end up together.
explanation: Anagrams share a signature: their sorted letters, or their 26 letter counts. Use the signature as a map key.
steps: For each word, compute key = [...w].sort().join('').
Push the word into map.get(key), creating the list if needed.
Return [...map.values()].
gotcha: A count-based key (26 numbers joined) avoids the sort and makes it O(n · k).
hint: What do all anagrams of a word have in common that you could use as a key?

title: Min stack
prompt: Build a stack with push, pop, top, and getMin, all in O(1).
explanation: Store the minimum at each level alongside each value. When you pop, the minimum below is already there.
steps: push(x): push [x, min(x, currentMin)].
pop: pop the pair.
getMin: read the second item of the top pair.
gotcha: A single min variable fails: after popping the minimum, you can't know the next one.
hint: After a pop, the old minimum must be available instantly. What could each entry remember?

title: Serialize and deserialize a binary tree
prompt: Turn a binary tree into a string, and that string back into the same tree.
explanation: A preorder DFS that writes a marker for every null child captures the exact shape. Deserialize by reading tokens in the same order.
steps: Serialize: preorder, writing the value or # for null, joined by commas.
Deserialize: split into tokens and keep a read index.
build(): read a token. If it's #, return null. Otherwise make a node, then left = build(), right = build().
gotcha: Without the null markers, different trees produce the same string.
hint: A traversal alone loses the shape. What extra marker would make it unambiguous?

title: Longest increasing subsequence
prompt: Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (not necessarily contiguous).
explanation: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i = 1 + the best dp[j] over earlier j with a smaller value. The O(n log n) version keeps a tails array and binary searches into it.
steps: dp filled with 1.
For each i, for each j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).
Return max(...dp).

complexity.time: O(n²), or O(n log n) with tails + binary search

gotcha: tails isn't the actual subsequence, just the smallest possible tail for each length.
hint: Define the answer for "ending at index i". How does it build on earlier indexes?

title: Word search II
prompt: Find every word from a list that can be traced on a letter grid through adjacent cells, using each cell at most once per word.
explanation: Put all the words in a trie, then DFS from each cell, walking the trie as you go. You search for every word at once and stop as soon as no word has the current prefix.
steps: Build a trie and store the full word at each end node.
DFS from each cell: follow the matching child, mark the cell as visited, recurse into its 4 neighbors, then unmark.
At a node with a word, record it and clear it so it isn't found twice.
gotcha: Searching each word separately (Word Search I in a loop) times out. The trie is the point.
hint: Searching for each word separately repeats work. How can you search for every prefix at once?

title: Find median from data stream
prompt: Numbers arrive one at a time. Support adding a number and asking for the current median.
explanation: Two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half. The median sits at their tops.
steps: Add to the max-heap, then move its top to the min-heap.
If the min-heap is now bigger, move its top back.
Median = top of the max-heap (odd count), or the average of both tops (even).
gotcha: Rebalance after every insert so the sizes never differ by more than 1.
hint: The median splits the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. What gives you each half's edge instantly?

title: Validate binary search tree
prompt: Is a binary tree a valid BST, with every left subtree smaller and every right subtree larger?
explanation: Pass down the allowed (min, max) range. Each node must fit its range, and its children inherit a narrower one. Alternatively, an inorder traversal must be strictly increasing.
steps: valid(node, lo = -Infinity, hi = Infinity).
If node.val <= lo || node.val >= hi, return false.
Recurse: valid(left, lo, node.val) && valid(right, node.val, hi).
gotcha: Checking each node only against its direct children is wrong. A deep node can break a limit set by an ancestor.
hint: A node deep in the left subtree has to respect limits from several ancestors. What could you pass down?
